1.note: Micah is using **with the rod they strike on the cheek** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they insult and humiliate him.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they utterly humiliate]

Micah is speaking of the surviving remnant of the people of Jerusalem (whom he previously called “daughter Zion”) as if they were a **daughter troop**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly as modeled in the UST.
The pronoun **He** refers to the enemy who is attacking Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Our enemy has laid siege against us]
By **us**, Micah means himself and the people of Jerusalem to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

2.note: **Bethlehem Ephrathah** is the name of a town located in a region of Judah (see it referenced in Matthew 2:6). **Ephrathah** distinguished it from another town called “Bethlehem” in the region of Zebulun. It is also called “the city of David” in Luke 2:4, since it was where David, king of Israel, was born.
The pronoun **me** refers to Yahweh, who is speaking these words through Micah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from you will come out for Yahweh]

Micah is using **his goings out** as a common expression of the culture to mean “his origin.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his origin is from ancient times]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the days before time began]

3.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun **them** refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will give the people of Israel up]

This prophecy appears to have two fulfillments. The first fulfillment would be when God brings the people of Israel back to their land. In this case, **the bearing one** would refer to “daughter Zion” 4:10, who stands for the faithful remnant of Israel. She **gives birth** to the restored nation of Israel. The second and greater fulfillment is when the mother of the Messiah gives birth to him who is able to create the new, fully restored people of God, bringing together the remnant of Israel and all of **his brothers** redeemed from the rest of mankind. If possible, translate this in a way that can apply to both fulfillments.
The pronoun **his** refers to the ruler whom Yahweh has promised. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the remainder of that ruler’s brothers]

Micah is speaking of the fellow Israelites of this ruler as if they were his **brothers**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the remainder of his fellow Israelites]

4.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the ruler that Yahweh promised to raise up from Bethlehem, whom Micah described in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the ruler will stand]

Micah is speaking of this ruler as if he would **shepherd** as one who cares for a flock of sheep. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will take his stand and lead and provide for his people]

Here, **the name of Yahweh** represents Yahweh himself and his authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the majestic authority of Yahweh his God]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of Israel, whom this ruler will shepherd. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the people of Israel will live securely]

5.note: Micah is speaking of this ruler bringing peace as if he were **peace** itself. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And this one will bring peace to his people]

The personal pronouns **he** and **him** throughout this verse refer to Assyria, which stands for the Assyrian army. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Assyria—when the Assyrian army comes into our land]
By **our** and **we**, Micah means himself and the people of Israel to whom he is speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Micah is speaking of the people choosing leaders as if they would **raise up** these leaders to a high place. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then we will choose to fight against them]

Micah is using **seven shepherds** and **eight princes of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as many leaders as will be needed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as many leaders as will be needed]

6.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the leaders mentioned in the previous verse who will fight against Assyria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And these leaders will shepherd]

Micah is speaking of these leaders ruling with military power as if they would **shepherd** them like a herd of sheep but in this context of the Assyrians, it would be **with a sword**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they will rule the land of Assyria with military power]

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will shepherd the land of Nimrod in its entrances]

Here, **the land of Nimrod** represents the territory that the ancient ruler Nimrod founded, that is, Assyria. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [which is the land that Nimrod founded,]

The phrase **in its entrances** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars have proposed that the original reading was a very similar word meaning “drawn sword,” which is represented in some ancient translations. You may want to follow this reading, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [with a drawn sword]
The pronoun **he** refers to the ruler whom Yahweh has promised. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the promised ruler will rescue us from Assyria]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remnant**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those of Jacob who remain]

Here, **Jacob** represents the descendants of Jacob, that is, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the remnant of the people of Israel]

The point of this comparison is that just as **dew** and **showers** come from Yahweh and refresh the grass, so the survivors of Israel will be a blessing to the many peoples among whom they live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [a blessing to them, like refreshing dew that comes from Yahweh, like showers on the grass]

The pronoun **that** refers to the **dew** and the **showers**, which come from Yahweh rather than from any human effort. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [moisture that does not wait for a man]

7.q: אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־יְקַוֶּה֙ לְ⁠אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְיַחֵ֖ל לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם
7.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [that does depend completely on Yahweh and not on people at all]

7.q: לֹֽא־יְקַוֶּה֙ לְ⁠אִ֔ישׁ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יְיַחֵ֖ל לִ⁠בְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם
7.note: Here, **a man** and **the sons of man** represent people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [does not wait for anyone and does not hope for any human being]

8.note: See how you translated the abstract noun **remnant** in 5:7.

8.q: כְּ⁠אַרְיֵה֙ בְּ⁠בַהֲמ֣וֹת יַ֔עַר כִּ⁠כְפִ֖יר בְּ⁠עֶדְרֵי צֹ֑אן
8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** is stronger than the other animals and **a young lion** can attack a flock of sheep without being stopped, so the survivors of Israel will be stronger than the peoples among whom they live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as strong as a lion among the animals of the forest, as unstoppable as a young lion among the flocks of sheep]

The terms **tramples** and **tears** mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [tears to pieces]

9.note: Some ancient manuscripts read according to the ULT. Other ancient manuscripts read “Your hand will rise over your adversaries, and all of your enemies will be cut off.” In that case, “your” could refer either to Yahweh or to Jacob, who represents his descendants. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Micah is saying what he wants Yahweh to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, I desire that your hand rise over your adversaries and that all your enemies be destroyed]

Here, **your hand** represents Yahweh’s power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May you triumph by your power over your adversaries]

The expression **be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may you cut off all of your enemies]

Micah is using **be cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may all of your enemies be destroyed]

10.note: Micah is using **on that day** as a common expression of the culture to mean “at that time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will be when that happens]
Micah is using **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here, **horses** and **chariots** represent “military power.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your military power and I will destroy your means of waging war]

The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Israel, whom Yahweh is addressing here. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your horses from your midst, people of Israel]

11.note: Yahweh is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will destroy]

12.note: Here, **your hand** represents “what you do.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [sorceries from what you do]

Yahweh is using **cut off** to mean “destroy” and **sorceries from your hand** to represent their power to practice witchcraft. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will destroy your power to practice sorcery]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorceries**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the practice of magic]

Yahweh is using **be to you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “you will no longer have.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will no longer have]

13.note: Yahweh is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy completely” or “get rid of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will wipe out] or [And I will get rid of]

To **bow down** was a symbolic action by which people showed reverence and submission. In this context, it was an action by which a person showed worship or submission to an idol. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and you will not submit yourselves]

Yahweh is using **the work of your hands** to represent the things that the people make and do, particularly idols and acts of worship directed toward them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the idols you make and worship]

14.note: Yahweh is speaking of the poles that the people use to worship the goddess Asherah as if they were plants that he would **uproot**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will tear out your Asherah poles]

15.note: Yahweh is using **in nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in anger]

The terms **nose** and **wrath** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [in furious anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in wrath I will avenge myself]

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that **listened** as it is used here, includes the meaning of “obeyed.” You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers as modeled in the UST.
